The diagnosis and management of pre-arthritic hip disease continues to evolve, and
surgical techniques have been considerably refined over the past several years. The
goals of surgical management are to alleviate pain, improve function, enhance quality of
life, and delay the progression of secondary osteoarthritis. Careful patient evaluation,
sound indications for surgical management, and precise surgical technique are the
fundamental principles of successful hip preservation procedures. Nonsurgical
management should be considered before surgical management. The hip arthroscopy
and periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) techniques described are those preferred by the
authors of this lesson; however, many variations exist and may be equally effective.
Surgical Management
Preoperative Planning for Hip Preservation Surgery
Preoperative planning is critical in hip preservation surgery.
Review of soft-tissue pathology (labrum, articular cartilage, ligamentum teres, capsule, etc.)
and underlying structural deformities (femoroacetabular impingement and hip
dysplasia/instability) is key to determining appropriate surgical management.
Careful assessment of patient history, physical examination, and preoperative imaging study
(radiographs, MRI, CT scans) findings determines the fundamental pathomechanics of the
hip, with a focus on determining the presence of instability and/or femoroacetabular
impingement (FAI).
If an appropriate course of nonsurgical management fails, surgical management is
considered. In patients with hip instability and acetabular dysplasia, PAO is considered to
stabilize the hip and normalize joint loading. Some patients have associated acetabular labral
tears that can be stabilized via concurrent hip arthroscopy.
Via an open approach to PAO, femoral head-neck offset deformities can be corrected to
prevent secondary hip impingement. In addition, preoperative three-dimensional imaging
studies can be obtained to identify patients who may require a proximal femur osteotomy as
an adjunct to PAO.
If a patient has clinical and radiographic findings of hip impingement without concomitant hip
dysplasia or signs of hip instability, hip arthroscopy via an all-arthroscopic approach is
indicated to repair the labrum and remove any hip impingement lesions, given the FAI
deformity is accessible arthroscopically.

For severe, non-focal FAI deformities, a surgical dislocation approach affords wide exposure
and access to these complex lesions.
Hip Arthroscopy
Multiple indications for hip arthroscopy exist, most notably FAI and labral tears.
Hip arthroscopy is performed through small incisions about the anterior and lateral hip using
arthroscopic instruments.
To access the hip joint, the femoral head is distracted using a special table and post or post-
less technology.
The central compartment and the peripheral compartment can be accessed via arthroscopic
hip techniques.
Complications, such as damage to nerves, including the pudendal nerve with traction and the
lateral femoral cutaneous nerve with surgical incisions, may occur.
In addition to the management of labral tears via hip arthroscopy, bony pathology deemed a
cause of a labral tear must be appropriately managed at time of surgery.
Mid- to long-term outcomes are associated with 80% to 90% survivorship for those with classic
indications.
Risk factors for failure include poor cartilage quality at the time of surgery and revision hip
surgery.
Indications
Symptomatic FAI
Hip dysplasia (in combination with structural deformity correction)
Symptomatic labral tears
Early articular cartilage disease: chondral flaps, chondromalacia
Osteochondritis dissecans
Hip capsule laxity
Iliopsoas bursitis
Synovitis and synovial disorders
Loose bodies
Ligamentum teres ruptures
Extra-articular hip disorders: internal or external hip snapping, abductor tears
Diagnostic evaluation of the hip

Central compartment: acetabular labrum; cartilage and bone, including the anterior inferior
iliac spine, femoral head cartilage, and ligamentum teres
Peripheral compartment: proximal femur head-neck junction, capsule, synovial disorders
Contraindications
Advanced degenerative joint disease
Disease states that limit arthroscopic access to the joint: morbid obesity, joint ankylosis,
heterotopic bone
Intra-articular hip disease (eg, labral tear) associated with major structural abnormalities
(acetabular dysplasia, Perthes-like deformities) that require correction of the underlying
structural bony problem
Complications
The surgical complication rate is relatively low (1% to 3%) for experienced hip arthroscopists.1
Traction injuries: generally transient, most commonly the pudendal nerve
Portal placement injuries
Accurate arthroscopic portal placement is important, given the proximity of several
neurovascular structures2 (Table 1).
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN) is at risk with use of the anterior portal; less
risk exists with use of the mid-anterior portal.
Other complications include deep vein thrombosis, instrument breakage, articular scuffing,
wound hematoma, intra-abdominal fluid extravasation, and infection.

Reproduced from Nepple, JJ, Clohisy JC, Schoemecker PL: Nonarthroplasty surgical
treatment of the hip, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 429-434.
A prospective multicenter study of 1,615 hips using a validated complication grading scheme
evaluated hip arthroscopy complications at a mean follow-up of 3 years. Of the procedures
reviewed (1,487 primary procedures and 128 revision arthroscopic procedures), FAI correction
was performed in 93.2% and labral repair was performed in 78.8%.1
The most common complication was postoperative LFCN disturbance (16.5%), with only 1.6%
persisting beyond 6 months. The rate of iatrogenic chondral injuries was 1.2%, iatrogenic
labral puncture was 0.9%, superficial portal infection was 1.1%, sensory deficits about the
foot was 0.8%, deep vein thrombosis was 0.1%, pulmonary embolism was 0.1%, perineal
(pudendal) nerve numbness was 1.4%, heterotopic ossification was 0.8%, and femoral neck
stress fractures was 0.1%.
No iatrogenic instability, osteonecrosis, or intra-abdominal fluid extravasation was reported
in this cohort.
Traction time longer than 60 minutes was associated with a substantially increased
complication rate (P < 0.0010).
A higher complication rate was reported in females (P = 0.17) compared with males.
The overall complication rate, exclusive of temporary lateral femoral cutaneous periportal
and thigh numbness, was 8.3% (grade 1 was 7.2%; grade 2 was 0.6%; grade 3 was 0.4%;
grade 4 was 0.1%). The major complication rate (grades 3 and 4) was 0.5%.
Outcomes
Systematic review of surgical management of FAI with a minimum follow-up of 2 years to
determine outcomes, complications, and modifiable modes of failure3
11 studies (9 were level IV, and 2 were level III) with a mean follow-up of 3.2 years (range, 2 to
5.2 years) were included.
Reduced pain and improved hip function were reported in 68% to 96% of patients.
Conversion to total hip arthroplasty (THA) was reported in 0 to 26% of the cases.

Major complications occurred in 0 to 18% of the procedures.
Radiographic osteoarthritis progression, which was reported in five studies, ranged from 0 to
33%.
52 hips in 50 patients with a mean age of 38 years were followed for a minimum of 10 years.4
Median improvement in modified Harris hip score was 25 points inclusive of THA and death
(56 preoperatively to 81 postoperatively; P = 0.02).
14 patients (26.9%) underwent conversion to THA, and two deaths occurred.
Four patients underwent repeat arthroscopy.
Two complications in one patient (neurapraxia of the LFCN, which persisted, and myositis
ossificans, which successfully resolved after treatment)
Radiograph demonstrating arthritis at the time of the index procedure is an indicator for
poor prognosis.
Retrospective analysis of prospectively collected data on arthroscopic management of FAI with
labral repair (n = 79 hips) or labral débridement (n = 75 hips);145 hips (94%) were followed for
a minimum of10 years.5
50 patients (34%) underwent THA within 10 years of arthroscopy.
Older patients (P < 0.001), hips with less than or equal to 2 mm joint space (P < 0.001), and
patients requiring microfracture (P = 0.036) had a significantly higher prevalence of
conversion to THA.
Labral repair (versus labral débridement) was not a predictor of outcome.
Surgical Technique
Patient Positioning
The most common technique involves supine patient positioning on a hip distraction table. Hip
arthroscopy–specific tables commonly are used (Resources 1 and 2).
Care should be taken to adequately pad the traction post for hip distraction. Injury to the
pudendal nerve is a relatively common complication during hip arthroscopy, and adequate
padding of the traction post can minimize this risk.
The patient’s surgical side arm is padded and positioned in adduction over the chest. The
patient’s nonsurgical leg is abducted approximately 30°, externally rotated, and flexed slightly.
The surgical side extremity is positioned in neutral abduction/adduction and slight hip flexion,
with approximately 10° of foot internal rotation.

Before surgical preparation, fluoroscopic images (AP-neutral, internal, and external rotation;
45° Dunn lateral and frog lateral) can be obtained. These images document the underlying
deformity and can be used as a reference during deformity correction. After surgical
sterilization, draping, and preoperative timeout, the no-fly zone, which extends from the
anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the patella, is marked.
To protect the femoral neurovascular bundle, no portals are made at or medial to this line.
Hip Joint Access/Exposure
Careful access to the hip joint is obtained via fluoroscopy and hip joint distraction.
The procedure begins with application of traction to the nonsurgical leg by a nonsterile
assistant. This traction is locked in place, and traction time is monitored throughout the
procedure.
Traction is then applied to the surgical extremity and the joint distracted 6 to 8 mm. A spinal
needle, nitinol guide wire, and cannulated trocar are used to establish the anterolateral portal
under fluoroscopic guidance. This portal entry site is just proximal and anterior to the greater
trochanter.
The anterolateral portal is established in the space between the labrum and the femoral head
created by application of traction. Care is taken to avoid damage to the femoral head and the
acetabular labrum (Resource 3).
A 70° arthroscope is commonly used to visualize all aspects of the joint.
An outflow portal comprised of a spinal needle also may be placed at this time in line with and
parallel to the instrumentation in the anterolateral portal at the posterior aspect of the greater
trochanter.
The field of vision is placed toward the anterior soft-tissue triangle created by the femoral
head, labrum, and joint capsule. The mid-anterior portal is then placed distally and medially at
the level of the skin, such that an equilateral triangle is made between the anterolateral portal,
the mid-anterior portal, and a point on the no-fly zone line.
During placement of the mid-anterior portal, care is taken to minimize injury to the LFCN.
After the cannula has successfully been introduced into the mid-anterior portal, a Beaver
blade (or capsular knife) is used to establish the interportal capsulotomy. The capsulotomy is
initially made anterior, taking care to protect and not injure the iliopsoas tendon. The
capsulotomy is extended lateral toward the anterolateral portal (Video 1). Care is taken to
ensure an adequate soft-tissue capsule cuff superiorly for later repair of the superior and
inferior capsular flaps.

The arthroscope can then be moved to the mid-anterior portal, and the lateral capsule and the
joint that surrounds the anterolateral hip joint access portal is visualized. The capsulotomy can
be extended laterally to complete the interportal capsulotomy.
Diagnostic Hip Arthroscopy
Careful and meticulous evaluation of intra-articular pathology is critical to identify all potential
sources of hip joint pain.
The authors of this lesson prefer the arthroscope in the anterolateral portal, and begin the
systematic, diagnostic portion of the procedure.
An arthroscopic probe is placed in the mid-anterior portal and is used to palpate the labrum
for possible tears and instability.
The authors of this lesson favor fixing tears that are unstable in nature. They also probe the
cartilage inferior to the labrum because this area can debond or detach from the underlying
bone in patients with FAI or hip dysplasia.

The remainder of the acetabular cartilage, the cartilage of the femoral head, and the
ligamentum teres are assessed. Arthroscopic images are obtained during this portion of the
procedure for documentation purposes.
Labral Repair
Labral repair is performed in patients with an unstable labral tear in whom the labral-chondral
complex is dissociated.
A combination of an arthroscopic shaver and arthroscopic electrocautery are used to lift the
hip capsule from the acetabular rim in the area on the extra-articular side of the labrum.
If the patient has a low-hanging anterior inferior iliac spine that is a source of subspine
impingement, then this region is decompressed before labral repair.
A high-speed burr can be used to remove any anterior inferior iliac spine prominence. After
the acetabular rim is exposed, a high-speed burr is used to prepare a bed for suture anchor
placement, labral repair, and healing.
Pincer lesions (as diagnosed preoperatively) are removed at this time with the use of the burr,
taking care to not introduce iatrogenic under-coverage via over-resection of the acetabular
rim.
A larger-bore working portal access sheath is placed in the mid-anterior portal. Anchors are
then placed on the exposed rim and pass the labral repair suture circumferentially around the
labrum.
In patients with adequate labral tissue, a base stitch technique, in which the labral repair
suture also is passed through the labrum itself to maintain an appropriate suction seal and
avoid an hourglass deformation of the labrum, can be used.
During placement of anchors, the arthroscope is toggled between visualization of the anchor
placement area on the acetabular rim and the joint itself to ensure no iatrogenic cartilage
injury with the anchor drill occurs.
Peripheral Compartment
Management of common bony pathology during hip arthroscopy is key to achieving good long-
term outcomes. Complete removal of common bone impinging lesions, or cam deformities, is
essential to optimize clinical outcomes and avoid symptom recurrence.
After the labrum has been adequately repaired and stabilized, attention is shifted to the
peripheral compartment to remove any peripheral compartment impinging bony lesions (cam
lesions).

Traction is slowly let down on the nonsurgical leg first and then the surgical leg. for the goal is
a total traction time of less 45 minutes for the central compartment, with most procedures
performed in approximately 30 minutes. After traction is let down, the hip is slowly flexed to
approximately 20° to 30° to perform the osteochondroplasty of the anterolateral head-neck
junction (cam lesion).
Fluoroscopy and an arthroscopic cautery wand can be used to mark the borders of the bony
area that will be resected.
An arthroscopic high-speed burr is used to carefully and sequentially recontour the head-neck
junction to a spherical shape.
Care is taken to not over-resect or create steep drop-offs in the contour of the resection that
may create iatrogenic hip instability or loss of the hip suction seal.
After appropriate resection is confirmed dynamically and via fluoroscopy, the arthroscopic
shaver is used to remove any bony debris from the hip joint. Intraoperative fluoroscopic
images are obtained to confirm and document adequate correction.
The hip capsule is repaired with the use of two to four nonabsorbable sutures tied
arthroscopically, and the skin is closed with the use of horizontal mattress sutures.
Periacetabular Osteotomy
Several indications for PAO exist, most commonly acetabular dysplasia.
The goal of PAO is to correct hip instability by increasing the weight-bearing surface area of the
acetabulum.
Traditional PAO involves the use of four osteotomies to mobilize the acetabular fragment.
PAO is associated with good mid- to long-term outcomes, with survivorship as high as 90%.
Complications include nonunion, nerve damage, and a risk of downstream osteoarthritis and
hip replacement despite correction of dysplasia.
Risk factors for failure include poor cartilage quality at the time of surgery, overcorrection, and
not managing other hip pathologies (impingement) concurrently.
Indications
Deficient anterolateral acetabular coverage of the femoral head resulting in symptoms from
structural hip instability and acetabular rim overload
True acetabular retroversion causing symptomatic pincer impingement (Figure 1)

Surgical Technique
PAO is a powerful surgical technique used to manage acetabular dysplasia (and associated
instability) and acetabular retroversion with associated pincer impingement (Videos 2 and 3).
The surgical technique requires surgical exposure, multiple pelvic osteotomies, acetabular
reorientation, surgical fixation, selective femoral head reshaping, and wound closure.

Exposure
PAO surgical exposure exposes the iliac crest and uses the classic, direct anterior approach to
the hip joint for the distal aspect.
An anterior approach to the hip is used via a modified Smith-Petersen interval for exposure.
The incision is C-shaped and begins proximally about the iliac crest and extends lateral to the
ASIS. The incision continues distal in a traditional Smith-Petersen orientation, aimed toward
the lateral patella.
Alternatively, a bikini-type incision may be used. Small subcutaneous flaps are raised
medially and laterally while avoiding the LFCN.
The fascia over the tensor fasciae latae muscle is incised in line with the muscle fibers, and
the muscle belly is retraced laterally.
The interval between the tensor fasciae latae and the sartorius is developed while protecting
the LFCN within the fascia overlying the sartorius. This dissection is then extended deep onto
the origin of the rectus femoris at the anterior inferior iliac spine.

Proximal to the ASIS, the external oblique muscle is reflected medially off the iliac crest. The
ASIS is then osteotomized and is reflected medially with the origin of the sartorius.
The conjoint tendon of the rectus muscle is identified at the anterior inferior iliac spine, and
dissection is carried along the medial edge of the rectus head and distal towards the hip
capsule. The iliocapsularis muscle fibers are reflected off the anterior hip capsule, and the
interval between the anterior hip capsule and the iliopsoas tendon is developed.
The plane between the anterior hip capsule and the iliopsoas tendon is followed inferiorly
and then posteriorly onto the anterior aspect of the ischium (infracotyloid groove).
A pair of large Metzenbaum scissors is then used to palpate the infracotyloid groove of the
ischium and identify the ischial osteotomy starting site.
Pelvic Osteotomies
Four separate osteotomies are made about the hip socket to free it for subsequent repositioning.
The osteotome position on the ischium is evaluated via AP and 50° oblique fluoroscopic views.
The infra-acetabular osteotomy starts just distal to the inferior lip of the acetabulum and is
aimed toward the central aspect of the ischial spine as visualized on the 50° oblique
fluoroscopic view. Three separate passes are made with this ischial cut: a medial, central, and
lateral pass. The lateral ischial cut passes the sciatic nerve at risk and should not be carried too
posterior or lateral.
Attention is then turned proximally to achieve the superior ramus cut. Hip flexion and
adduction of the surgical leg are achieved to relax soft-tissue structures overlying the superior
ramus. The iliopsoas and the femoral neurovascular bundle are retracted medially, taking care
to minimize traction time and force. The superior pubic ramus is exposed circumferentially,
and the osteotomy is made just medial to the iliopectineal eminence with a straight 0.5-inch
osteotome. The obturator nerve is protected with the use of circumferential retractors.
The osteotomy of the ilium is performed next, after subperiosteal exposure of the medial
ilium. The hip is flexed and adducted to improve visualization, and the iliac cut is made
through the midsubstance of the ASIS osteotomy bed, directly toward the sciatic notch. Medial
and lateral cortex osteotomies are completed and stop approximately 1 cm lateral to the
pelvic brim.
The posterior column is exposed with the use of an angled cobra retractor, and the posterior
column cut is made with the goal of bisecting the posterior column between the articular
surface anteriorly and the posterior cortex. The authors of this lesson prefer a long, slightly
curved 0.5-inch osteotome and fluoroscopic guidance for this cut.

After completion of the periacetabular cuts, a partially threaded Schanz pin is placed into the
acetabular fragment in the supra-acetabular region, and the mobility of the fragment is
confirmed. A large, universal reduction clamp is placed around the iliac portion of the
acetabular fragment and the Schanz pin, allowing for the acetabular fragment to be mobilized.
Manipulation of the fragment is performed to optimize mobility for reduction of the
acetabulum.
Acetabular Reorientation and Fixation
Reorientation of the acetabulum is specific to the patient and attempts to normalize hip joint
structure and biomechanics.
In classic acetabular dysplasia, the acetabulum usually is repositioned with adduction (lateral
coverage), internal rotation (maintenance of anteversion), and some forward tilt or extension
(anterior coverage). The fragment is then translated medially if the hip joint center was lateral
at baseline. The fragment is then fixed with the use of two 3/32-inch (0.24-cm) Kirschner wires.
Acetabular reduction is assessed intraoperatively via fluoroscopy to ensure accurate reduction
(Resource 4). Initial fluoroscopy assessment included obtaining a high-quality AP image
centered over the symphysis pubis. This image should emulate the preoperative standing AP
radiograph. Acetabular reduction is assessed initially via an AP fluoroscopic view, evaluating
the lateral center edge angle, acetabular inclination, medial translation of the hip-joint center,
the position of the teardrop, and version of the acetabulum.
After complete fluoroscopic assessment, the acetabulum may need to be repositioned to
achieve optimal deformity correction. The repositioned hip socket is then fixed with the use of
four 4.5-mm cortical screws. One screw is placed into the anterolateral aspect of the
acetabular fragment to act as a blocking screw. Two or three additional screws are placed
progressively more medially. If necessary, a screw also can be placed from the anterior
acetabular fragment into the ilium.
Femoral Head Reshaping
A femoral head osteochondroplasty is performed selectively (in approximately 75% of
patients) to optimize clinical outcomes and avoid secondary FAI after the PAO.
After appropriate acetabular reorientation and fixation is confirmed, hip motion is assessed.
A minimum of 90° of hip flexion must be obtained after acetabular correction. If internal

and correct the head-neck offset deformity.
An anterior I-shaped arthrotomy is performed, with medial and lateral flaps of the hip
capsule raised to provide access to the head-neck junction.
Lack of femoral head-neck offset is managed via osteochondroplasty. This is a common
concomitant deformity in dysplastic hips that may result in anterior FAI postoperatively.
The osteoplasty is performed with the use of a 0.5-inch (1.27-cm) curved osteotome and
burr. The excess osteochondral tissue is resected at the anterolateral head-neck junction to
create improved offset and femoral head sphericity.
After osteochondroplasty, hip flexion motion is assessed and confirmed to be improved.
The authors of this lesson also perform a final fluoroscopic assessment of the head-neck
junction to confirm appropriate recontouring. In patients with severe femoral deformity, a
proximal femur osteotomy may be necessary and is determined preoperatively. Patients with
severely dysplastic hips may have a valgus proximal femur deformity and/or excessive
femoral antetorsion that may require a varus-producing, derotation intertrochanteric
osteotomy.
Wound Closure
Meticulous closure is performed, including repair of the ASIS osteotomy.
After thorough irrigation of the wound, the anterior hip capsule is approximated with the use
of absorbable suture.
The site of the ASIS osteotomy is then repaired with the use of nonabsorbable suture through
drill holes in the ilium.
The remainder of the superficial wound is closed in a routine fashion, taking care to close in
progressive, deep to superficial layers.
